rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that federal uniformity does not help because employer behavior still varies
rebuttals.objection: Uniformity of the holiday itself matters because it provides a consistent nationwide standard that reduces scheduling barriers across states, instead of leaving access entirely to patchwork local rules.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday reduces time pressure by changing schedules and logistics
rebuttals.objection: For low-wage workers the binding constraint is still whether they are scheduled to work during voting hours or can take paid/flexible time, so school or transit changes do not reliably give them actual voting time.

rebuttals.target: AG1's argument that a holiday complements other reforms rather than substituting for them
rebuttals.objection: A holiday can dilute pressure for the enforceable reforms that actually protect workers, because once Election Day is labeled a holiday, policymakers may treat the problem as solved and fail to adopt stronger time-off or early-voting protections.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday creates uniform access
rebuttals.objection: A national holiday only creates a uniform calendar change, not uniform employer obligations, so the key variable—whether an hourly worker can actually take time off—still depends on the workplace.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that a holiday is too blunt because it will not guarantee paid time off for every worker
rebuttals.objection: Many employers close or reduce hours on federal holidays, so the policy changes the default schedule and removes the workday conflict for many workers even if paid leave is not guaranteed everywhere.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that the holiday would distract from better reforms
rebuttals.objection: Opposing the holiday because it is not the only solution is too demanding; supporting it does not prevent stronger reforms from also being enacted, and it can be an incremental improvement rather than a replacement for other measures.

rebuttals.target: AG2's concern that a holiday would not reduce waiting or election congestion
rebuttals.objection: A national holiday can actually help polling operations by giving jurisdictions more flexibility to staff polls and manage turnout without competing with normal school and work schedules, which may reduce practical barriers like long lines.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday changes the default schedule enough to help workers
rebuttals.objection: Essential and service jobs still run on holidays, so the core constraint for low-income hourly workers remains whether they can safely leave work or receive paid/flexible time; a holiday does not reliably change that reality.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday reduces time pressure and logistics overall
rebuttals.objection: A holiday can concentrate voting demand on one day, which may increase lines and waiting times at polling places and shift the time squeeze from work schedules to polling-place congestion.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday is a worthwhile incremental step
rebuttals.objection: Making a federal calendar change the headline policy misallocates effort when more direct levers—state time-off-to-vote rules, expanded early voting or vote-by-mail, and streamlined administration—address the binding constraint more effectively.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that some workers still having to work defeats the holiday's value
rebuttals.objection: The holiday does not have to solve every worker's problem to matter; it can still reduce barriers for millions by making voting more compatible with school and workplace schedules.

rebuttals.target: AG2's argument that congestion makes a holiday counterproductive
rebuttals.objection: Even if turnout is concentrated on the holiday, election administrators can better staff polling places and voters are less constrained by after-work and school-related timing, so the system can manage the day more effectively.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that a holiday would distract from stronger reforms
rebuttals.objection: That is an implementation concern, not a reason to oppose the baseline benefit; a holiday can be enacted alongside employer time-off rules, early voting, vote-by-mail, and administrative fixes.

rebuttals.target: AG2's assumption that a holiday cannot help unless it fully solves access
rebuttals.objection: A holiday can still reduce practical barriers such as line management and election-day operations, giving jurisdictions more capacity to handle turnout without competing with ordinary school and work congestion.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that better election administration and many workers benefiting make the holiday worthwhile
rebuttals.objection: Improved poll staffing does not solve the core time-off problem for low-income hourly workers, because they still need the ability to leave work safely and without losing pay; a holiday does not reliably provide that.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that the policy is acceptable because it helps many workers
rebuttals.objection: The distributional problem remains: a holiday may mainly help people with flexible jobs or jobs that close, while leaving inflexible hourly workers with the same constraints, potentially widening rather than reducing gaps in participation.

rebuttals.target: AG1's argument that a holiday is worthwhile when paired with other reforms
rebuttals.objection: If the holiday only matters when combined with enforceable time-off rules, expanded early voting, and administrative fixes, then it is an inefficient centerpiece compared with direct reforms that address the barrier without relying on a calendar change.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday directly removes the work-schedule barrier that keeps millions from voting.
rebuttals.objection: A federal holiday does not compel private employers to give paid time off or shut down, so many hourly retail and service workers would still be scheduled to work and would still face difficulty voting during limited polling hours. Therefore, the holiday would not reliably eliminate the scheduling barrier and could leave workers with lost wages or pressure to vote in narrow windows instead.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday will create a practical day-off window for voters because schools close and many workplaces follow holiday norms.
rebuttals.objection: Even if schools close, federal holiday status does not legally require private employers to close or provide paid leave. In practice, many service and retail workplaces remain open or partially staffed, so the workers most constrained by work schedules may still face the same voting conflict.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s implication that because many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, an Election Day holiday is a workable way to reduce scheduling barriers in the U.S.
rebuttals.objection: The fact that some other democracies use weekend or holiday elections does not show that a U.S. federal holiday would reliably overcome work-schedule barriers here, since private employers would still not be required to give paid time off or close.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s view that an Election Day holiday is a primary solution to turnout barriers.
rebuttals.objection: A holiday only addresses a single day-of scheduling constraint and does not fix other major obstacles, especially pre-election administrative problems like registration issues. Reforms such as automatic voter registration or state-level time-off protections are more direct and reliable.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday directly targets the most immediate reason low-income voters fail to participate.
rebuttals.objection: For many low-income voters, the real obstacle is not just the date itself but the fact that federal holiday status does not require paid leave or schedule changes from private employers. If they still must work or lose wages, the holiday does not meaningfully remove the barrier.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s idea that turning Election Day into a shared civic event lowers social cost enough to increase turnout even for people with multiple obstacles.
rebuttals.objection: The normalization or civic-celebration effect does not reliably produce actual voting follow-through when the dominant constraint remains lost wages and limited polling hours. Without employer-mandated time off, framing Election Day as an event does not solve the practical barrier.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and increase turnout
rebuttals.objection: A federal national holiday does not require private employers to close or to provide paid time off, so it would not reliably give hourly retail and service workers time off to vote.

rebuttals.target: AG1's assumption that a holiday would broadly solve the day-of scheduling problem for people who work or go to school
rebuttals.objection: Low-income workers are disproportionately concentrated in hourly retail and service jobs that often still require work on holidays and offer little flexibility, so those workers would remain especially burdened.

rebuttals.target: AG1's conclusion that a holiday, by itself, is an effective voting-access reform
rebuttals.objection: If the key scheduling barriers for the hardest-hit workers are not actually eliminated, then making Election Day a holiday will not reliably increase voting access or turnout on its own.

rebuttals.target: AG1's turnout argument for an Election Day holiday
rebuttals.objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

rebuttals.target: AG1's proposal that a national holiday is the best reform to prioritize
rebuttals.objection: More reliable alternatives exist, such as state laws requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration, which directly reduce barriers without depending on whether private employers treat Election Day like a holiday.

rebuttals.target: AG1's broader conclusion that Election Day should be a national holiday
rebuttals.objection: A policy is especially problematic when it disadvantages low-income workers and is unlikely to produce reliable turnout gains by itself, so Election Day should not be a national holiday.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that state-by-state employer time-off reforms are insufficient only because they vary by state
rebuttals.objection: Policies that depend on private employer time-off or state-by-state compliance cannot guarantee that the day-of scheduling conflict is removed for millions nationwide, whereas a holiday still leaves employer discretion in place.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a national holiday uniformly removes the scheduling conflict
rebuttals.objection: A national holiday is only a calendar change; even if schools and some workplaces reduce operations, private employers are not required to close or adjust schedules, so the conflict is not eliminated uniformly.

rebuttals.target: AG1's assumption that solving the day-of schedule is enough to ensure voting access
rebuttals.objection: Voting access also depends on being registered or otherwise eligible in time to cast a ballot, and a holiday does nothing by itself to solve those pre-Election Day barriers.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday is the most reliable access reform
rebuttals.objection: Automatic voter registration directly increases advance registration, so a holiday cannot itself reliably eliminate major barriers the way other reforms can.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday should be preferred even if it only addresses one barrier
rebuttals.objection: A policy that cannot reliably eliminate major voting barriers should not replace more direct reforms when the goal is improving access.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday is the most reliable way to address work-hour voting barriers
rebuttals.objection: The most reliable way to reduce work-hour voting barriers is to legally require employer time off, not to rely on employers choosing to accommodate a holiday.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that holiday status will meaningfully change schedules for workers
rebuttals.objection: A federal Election Day holiday does not legally require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so it leaves employer discretion intact.

rebuttals.target: AG1's assumption that low-income workers will benefit enough from a holiday to make it a good reform
rebuttals.objection: Because low-income workers are concentrated in hourly retail and service jobs with limited flexibility, employer discretion means many of them would still be scheduled to work or would lose pay on Election Day.

rebuttals.target: AG1's equity argument for a national holiday
rebuttals.objection: If a voting-access policy does not reliably remove the key work-time barrier for low-income hourly workers, then it is an unreliable and inequitable reform.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday is preferable to other reforms
rebuttals.objection: State voter time-off laws and automatic voter registration are more reliable because they directly reduce voting barriers through enforceable requirements rather than depending on private employers treating the day as a holiday.

rebuttals.target: AG1's conclusion that the holiday is justified by access alone
rebuttals.objection: A voting-access reform that is unreliable for low-income workers should not be preferred over more reliable barrier-reduction reforms.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday reduces scheduling conflicts in practice
rebuttals.objection: For many voters, the real issue is whether they can take time off during work hours without losing pay or lacking legally guaranteed time off; simply calling Election Day a holiday does not guarantee that.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that low-income workers will particularly benefit from a holiday
rebuttals.objection: Because low-income hourly workers still depend on employer discretion and often lack flexibility, a holiday does not reliably remove the work-time conflict that blocks their voting.

rebuttals.target: AG1's broader conclusion that the holiday is an equitable voting-access reform
rebuttals.objection: If a policy does not reliably remove the work-time barrier for low-income hourly workers, it is an unreliable and inequitable way to improve voting access.

rebuttals.target: AG1's final claim that a national holiday should be preferred over other reforms
rebuttals.objection: A reform that is unreliable for low-income workers should not be preferred over approaches that directly require employer time off or improve registration through enforceable system changes.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday standardizes access across workers
rebuttals.objection: Even if a federal holiday changes school and some workplace schedules, it still does not guarantee paid time off or closure from private employers, so it is not a fully reliable schedule solution.

rebuttals.target: AG1's equity claim that a holiday especially helps workers with the fewest schedule options
rebuttals.objection: Because low-income hourly workers cannot easily rearrange their schedules and depend heavily on fixed routines, an employer-by-employer system is less fair than a policy that legally requires time off.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday elevates civic participation and is therefore justified
rebuttals.objection: Designating a holiday may signal civic celebration, but that symbolic framing does not answer the practical objection that the policy still fails to reliably solve the voting-access problem.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that bipartisan and international support makes a holiday the right reform
rebuttals.objection: The existence of public support or of other countries using holiday or weekend elections does not show that the policy is effective at increasing turnout or access in the U.S. context.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove major scheduling barriers and make voting easier for everyone.
rebuttals.objection: Declaring Election Day a federal holiday would not reliably solve the scheduling problem because federal law does not require private employers to give paid time off or close. Many workers in retail, food service, hospitals, and similar jobs would still be scheduled to work, so the holiday would not guarantee time to vote.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s assumption that an Election Day holiday would broadly help voters rather than create new burdens.
rebuttals.objection: A holiday could disadvantage low-income workers: salaried or unionized employees may benefit from existing holiday policies, while hourly workers may still have to work or may lose pay if they are given unpaid time off. So the policy may help some people more than others and can leave the lowest-income workers no better off.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s implication that a holiday is the best or most reliable way to improve voting access.
rebuttals.objection: State-level reforms that directly require employer accommodations for voting, such as guaranteed time off or paid leave, are more dependable than merely making Election Day a holiday because they directly address the work-schedule barrier.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s broader claim that an election holiday is an effective turnout reform.
rebuttals.objection: Research suggests that simply declaring an election holiday is less effective at increasing turnout than targeted access measures such as guaranteed time to vote, expanded early voting, vote-by-mail, and automatic voter registration.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday changes the default scheduling environment enough to solve the problem.
rebuttals.objection: The core problem is low-wage, hourly, customer-facing workers who are least able to take time off and whose workplaces often do not close on holidays. A holiday label does not require those employers to stop operations or provide paid time, so the key barrier remains for the workers most in need of help.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s argument that a holiday reduces barriers by shifting the day into a more supportive environment for families and workers.
rebuttals.objection: The holiday can shift the burden onto low-income workers by creating unpaid time-off risks and lost wages, meaning it may reduce barriers for some while leaving the most vulnerable workers in essentially the same position or worse.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s suggestion that a national holiday creates a consistent baseline for access.
rebuttals.objection: A calendar change is mostly symbolic unless it comes with a legal requirement for paid or job-protected time to vote. A rule that directly mandates voting time is more consistent and more likely to benefit low-income workers than simply changing the holiday status.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a holiday improves logistics such as childcare and weekday routines.
rebuttals.objection: That argument can cut the other way: low-cost childcare tied to school schedules may close or reduce hours on holidays, and essential retail/service workers still have to work. As a result, low-income families may face higher childcare costs or no workable coverage.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s position that a holiday is useful as a complement to other reforms.
rebuttals.objection: If the country still needs paid or job-protected time off and other concrete access reforms to ensure low-income workers can vote, then making Election Day a national holiday is largely redundant and risks being misleading as a centerpiece policy.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s view that a holiday meaningfully changes incentives even without forcing employers to close or pay holiday wages.
rebuttals.objection: Because private employers are not required to close or provide holiday pay, many hourly workers would still face the same wage tradeoff or the loss of hours. In practice, people whose employers already offer holiday time would benefit more, so the policy does not reliably target the biggest turnout barriers for low-income voters.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s broader assumption that holiday status would meaningfully change daytime availability for most voters
rebuttals.objection: Even if some schools close, a federal holiday does not legally require private employers to close or pay workers, so millions of hourly workers in retail, food service, caregiving, and other sectors would still have to work. For low-income workers facing the tightest time constraints, the main obstacle would remain in place, so a holiday is not a reliable scheduling solution.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s claim that only direct voting-logistics reforms address the problem
rebuttals.objection: The scheduling barrier includes school and childcare constraints, not just employer rules. If Election Day is a national holiday, schools close and childcare arrangements shift, which directly helps parents and caregivers who otherwise must choose between voting and their daytime responsibilities. So the holiday does address a major part of the timing problem.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would improve access for many people by changing schools and workplace schedules
rebuttals.objection: Research and experience suggest that an election-day-only holiday is a weak turnout strategy by itself; it does not directly change the key barriers that keep people from voting, especially for working people. More effective reforms are those that explicitly reduce voting friction, such as employer time-off laws or automatic voter registration.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s preference for a holiday over targeted reforms
rebuttals.objection: State laws requiring employers to provide time off for voting, and automatic voter registration, are more reliable solutions than a federal holiday. They directly address the relevant barriers—time off and registration—rather than assuming a holiday will indirectly improve access.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would be a reliable “day available” for voting
rebuttals.objection: The argument assumes that holiday designation will actually make workplaces and school/childcare schedules change in practice for most constrained voters, but that is not guaranteed. Because private employers are not required to close or offer paid leave, and childcare routines may not shift uniformly nationwide, a national holiday does not reliably create a society-wide day off for voting.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not reliably create time off because employer closure is not mandated
rebuttals.objection: The decisive issue is not only whether every private employer must close, but whether the holiday changes the real-world scheduling environment enough to let many working and parenting households vote. Since many workplaces follow holiday schedules and schools/childcare arrangements shift, the holiday still creates a broad day of availability and thus directly addresses the scheduling barrier.

rebuttals.target: AG2’s objection that low-income workers would still be scheduled and therefore would not benefit meaningfully
rebuttals.objection: The holiday would help precisely because the main obstacle is not just employer mandates in the abstract; it is the need to coordinate work, school, childcare, and transportation during a limited in-person voting window. By changing the day structure that governs those routines, Election Day as a holiday creates a practical opportunity to vote that the current schedule does not provide.

rebuttals.target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is uniquely suited to helping people most harmed by work and school schedules
rebuttals.objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee that school and childcare routines will shift uniformly or that private employers will provide time off, so it does not reliably produce a society-wide day available for voting. Because the most constrained voters can still be working or otherwise tied to their usual routines, the holiday is not uniquely suited to the scheduling barrier in the way claimed.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and give workers practical time to vote
rebuttals.objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or give paid time off, so many low-income retail and service workers would still have to work and would not reliably gain time to vote.

rebuttals.target: AG1's assumption that a holiday would broadly help the voters most constrained by work schedules
rebuttals.objection: Low-income workers are concentrated in retail and service jobs that often still operate on federal holidays, meaning the people most likely to face access barriers would often still be scheduled to work on Election Day.

rebuttals.target: AG1's conclusion that a holiday would improve voting access for low-income workers
rebuttals.objection: Because many low-income workers would still need to work and would not be guaranteed paid time off, the holiday could leave the original time barrier in place while adding a lost-wages tradeoff, which may disadvantage them.

rebuttals.target: AG1's broader claim that the holiday would increase turnout and access more effectively than other reforms
rebuttals.objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday changes scheduling norms enough to solve access problems
rebuttals.objection: Many low-income workers in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and other customer-facing jobs are still needed on federal holidays, so the holiday would not reliably reduce their daytime work obligations enough to make voting easy.

rebuttals.target: AG1's assumption that a holiday removes the practical time barrier for low-income workers
rebuttals.objection: If workers still have to work and do not have guaranteed paid time off to vote, they must either vote outside work hours or take unpaid time off, so the time/scheduling barrier remains rather than being removed.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that the holiday would help low-income workers rather than hurt them
rebuttals.objection: For low-income workers, needing to choose between voting and losing pay creates a pay-versus-time tradeoff that can persist even if some employers are lenient, so the policy may disadvantage them instead of helping them.

rebuttals.target: AG1's suggestion that the holiday is the right solution because it helps workers vote
rebuttals.objection: More reliable alternatives exist, such as state laws requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration, because these directly address access barriers instead of depending on employers' voluntary schedule changes.

rebuttals.target: AG1's premise that making Election Day a holiday reduces congestion by dispersing voters
rebuttals.objection: A holiday is likely to increase same-day in-person voting demand, and since election resources are finite, that added demand can increase wait times at polling places.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that reduced congestion would help low-income voters
rebuttals.objection: Low-income workers already bear higher time costs from delays and often have fewer alternative voting options, so longer waits on a holiday could worsen the practical barriers they face.

rebuttals.target: AG1's broader conclusion that the holiday is a good nationwide solution
rebuttals.objection: Because the holiday risks creating longer waits through same-day congestion and disproportionately burdens voters with less flexibility, it should not be adopted as a nationwide policy.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a holiday would disperse voting enough to reduce crowding
rebuttals.objection: Even if overall demand is spread across the day, low-income shift workers still face narrow voting windows before, after, or during short breaks, so effective demand remains concentrated for them.

rebuttals.target: AG1's assumption that dispersing turnout across the day solves access problems
rebuttals.objection: If voters' usable time is concentrated into narrow windows, polling-place capacity limits can still produce long waits in those windows, so the holiday may not actually improve access for low-income workers.

rebuttals.target: AG1's conclusion that holiday-driven line reduction will help the most time-constrained voters
rebuttals.objection: Long waits still impose a high net time cost on low-income voters, who have less flexibility and fewer ways to absorb delays, so the holiday can worsen access for the people most constrained by time.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that an election holiday meaningfully increases turnout
rebuttals.objection: Research says an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms, so any benefit from the holiday alone is likely limited.

rebuttals.target: AG1's idea that broad public support and OECD practice make the holiday a good policy
rebuttals.objection: Even if a policy is popular or common elsewhere, it still should not be adopted if it does not reliably improve voting access for the constrained voters it is meant to help.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that the turnout evidence against a holiday does not apply because a holiday changes scheduling norms
rebuttals.objection: The evidence against an election holiday by itself only matters if the holiday does not meaningfully change people's feasible voting time, so merely calling it a holiday does not answer the turnout objection.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would create practical time for people to vote
rebuttals.objection: A holiday does not guarantee that private employers will provide paid time off or close, so many low-income shift workers would still have to work or would need to vote at the cost of lost earnings.

rebuttals.target: AG1's claim that civic-celebration and motivation effects make the holiday worthwhile
rebuttals.objection: Motivational or civic-importance effects only matter when people have feasible time to act on them without prohibitive earnings loss or disruption, which many constrained workers would not have.

rebuttals.target: AG1's overall conclusion that the holiday would improve voting access
rebuttals.objection: Even if some institutions reduce obligations, the holiday's main mechanism still does not reliably deliver workable access for the low-income workers it is supposed to help and may leave their barriers unchanged or worse.

rebuttals.target: AG1's final policy recommendation
rebuttals.objection: A nationwide holiday should not be adopted when it does not reliably improve access for constrained voters and can predictably worsen their barriers through time-and-earnings tradeoffs.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday does not help because it does not guarantee paid time off from private employers
rebuttals.objection: The proposal is about reducing scheduling conflicts, not guaranteeing paid time off for every private employee; a policy can still improve access by creating reduced-obligation norms and practical time windows.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that low-income workers would not benefit because they may still have to work
rebuttals.objection: A national holiday would change scheduling expectations for schools and many workplaces and would remove the barrier for a large number of people, even if some specific workers still work.

rebuttals.target: AG2's assumption that lack of universal paid leave defeats the proposal
rebuttals.objection: The holiday does not need to help every voter equally to be worthwhile; it only needs to meaningfully reduce scheduling barriers for millions of Americans.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that federal holiday status does not materially reduce work conflicts
rebuttals.objection: Designating Election Day a national holiday changes how institutions and employers plan the day, creating a baseline expectation of reduced obligations that can give many voters practical time to vote.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that low-income workers would still face the same access barriers
rebuttals.objection: Even for retail and service workers, holiday-driven schedule changes can reduce hours or shift obligations enough to lessen the time-and-scheduling barrier rather than leaving it unchanged.

rebuttals.target: AG2's argument that the holiday would disadvantage low-income workers
rebuttals.objection: The holiday also frames voting as a civic celebration and can increase participation, so it is not merely a cost to low-income workers but also a mechanism for easier voting and stronger civic engagement.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that a holiday would make polling-place congestion worse for low-income voters
rebuttals.objection: If Election Day is a holiday, voters who otherwise cannot leave work gain more practical time slots to vote across the day, which should spread demand rather than concentrate it.

rebuttals.target: AG2's assumption that same-day demand would necessarily create worse waits
rebuttals.objection: Polling-place crowding is worst when demand is compressed into narrow time windows, so dispersing voters over the day reduces peak congestion and the risk of long lines.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that low-income voters would be harmed by a holiday's polling lines
rebuttals.objection: Reducing peak congestion would lower the time-cost burden on low-income voters, making them less likely to be harmed by lines and more likely to see improved access.

rebuttals.target: AG2's turnout-based objection that holidays do not work by themselves
rebuttals.objection: The turnout critique assumes the holiday does not change scheduling norms, but a national holiday would prompt schools and workplaces to treat the day as one with reduced obligations, creating real time to vote.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that a holiday is just a symbolic label
rebuttals.objection: A national Election Day holiday is more than symbolism because it alters institutions' scheduling and gives many people workable voting time.

rebuttals.target: AG2's contention that the holiday does not address the main barrier
rebuttals.objection: The main barrier the proposal targets is the conflict between school/work schedules and voting times, so reducing those conflicts directly improves access.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that civic celebration is irrelevant to turnout
rebuttals.objection: Making voting feel like a civic celebration rather than a chore increases the perceived importance of voting and strengthens participation incentives.

rebuttals.target: AG2's suggestion that public support and international practice do not help the case
rebuttals.objection: The proposal has broad public support and matches common practice in peer democracies, which supports adopting it rather than treating it as an outlier.

rebuttals.target: AG2's claim that the holiday inherently worsens access for constrained voters
rebuttals.objection: The predicted harm is not established against the mechanism by which a holiday changes scheduling norms and expands workable voting time.
